item.title: Fuel price hike looms
item.description: FUEL prices are expected to rise again next month due to ongoing international tensions in the Middle East. Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said the Government had been informed of the expected increase, which was linked to overseas developments.
item.content:encoded:
FUEL prices are expected to rise again next month due to ongoing international tensions in the Middle East.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said the Government had been informed of the expected increase, which was linked to overseas developments.

“There has been an increase in the prices of goods. Yesterday we were told that the price of fuel would increase,” he said.

Mr Rabuka said the increase was being driven by international conflicts that had pushed up global fuel prices, which were beyond the Government’s control.

“We thought the increase in fuel prices would stop.”

Mr Rabuka made the comments while speaking at the launch of the Fiji Blue Economy and Green Growth Community Development Program at Koronatoga Village in Cakaudrove yesterday.

He said international events continued to have a direct impact on Fiji’s economy, particularly through higher fuel costs, which also affected the prices of goods and services.

Fuel prices in Fiji are reviewed monthly by the Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission based on changes in international refined fuel prices, freight costs and the exchange rate.

The next fuel price announcement is expected at the end of the month.

item.title: Rabuka defends cost of CoI
item.description: MONEY spent on the Commission of Inquiry was not wasted because ensuring good governance is worth the investment, Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says. Mr Rabuka defended the estimated $2million spent on the Commission of Inquiry (CoI), saying the process was never intended to prosecute anyone but to investigate allegations and establish the facts.
item.content:encoded:
MONEY spent on the Commission of Inquiry was not wasted because ensuring good governance is worth the investment, Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says.

Mr Rabuka defended the estimated $2million spent on the Commission of Inquiry (CoI), saying the process was never intended to prosecute anyone but to investigate allegations and establish the facts.

“It’s not wasted. Any amount of money spent on ensuring good governance is justifiable,” Mr Rabuka said.

Responding to questions on claims that the inquiry had concluded without enough evidence to lay charges, Mr Rabuka said there was a misunderstanding about the role of the commission.

“Well, the Court of Inquiry or the Commission of Inquiry is not a prosecutorial process. They are not there to prosecute,” he said.

“It is inquisitorial. They are doing an inquisition, like investigative. After the investigation, then you put it to those that will progress it to the prosecution level.”

Mr Rabuka said the commission’s responsibility was to establish what had occurred and determine whether any findings pointed to possible breaches of the law.

He said the $5000-a-day payment for CoI commissioner Justice David Ashton-Lewis was part of a deal approved by Cabinet before he was appointed.

Mr Rabuka made the comments when asked if he was aware of the payment made to the retired Australian judge who led the Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption commissioner Barbara Malimali.

He said Cabinet had approved the terms of Justice Ashton-Lewis’ appointment before the inquiry began.

item.title: CJ urges lawyers to maintain ethical standards
item.description: CHIEF Justice Salesi Temo has urged new lawyers to build their reputations through honesty and never to step outside “the four corners of the law” even when pressured by clients. Speaking to 11 newly- admitted lawyers yesterday, Justice Temo said legal practitioners must remain committed to ethical practices while advocating fearlessly for those they represent.
item.content:encoded:
CHIEF Justice Salesi Temo has urged new lawyers to build their reputations through honesty and never to step outside “the four corners of the law” even when pressured by clients.

Speaking to 11 newly- admitted lawyers yesterday, Justice Temo said legal practitioners must remain committed to ethical practices while advocating fearlessly for those they represent.

He said a lawyer’s conduct in the courtroom played a significant role in earning the respect of the bench.

“I’ve come through lawyers who fight fearlessly but are not polite in the courtroom and I’ve come through lawyers who are very polite in the courtroom,” he said.

Justice Temo said, in his view, the most effective lawyers were those who remained courteous.

He said politeness could be a powerful advocacy tool, admitting there had been occasions when he later questioned decisions he had made after being persuaded by courteous counsel.

“You are in the courtroom, you are nothing but an advocate.

“Your clients. You are not there to decide for them. The one who’s going to decide is the one who sits on the bench.”

He said lawyers should focus on persuading the court through professional advocacy while recognising that judges closely observe their conduct.

“For us on the bench, we observe you lawyers as you appear before us. Reputation is what you build in the courtroom.”

Justice Temo said a strong reputation was earned through hard work, honesty and courage, but stressed that lawyers must always operate within the law.

He also cautioned the new lawyers against giving in to pressure from clients to act improperly.

“Some of your clients may try and persuade you to work outside the four corners of the law. Please don’t go that way. Stay within the four corners,” he said.

item.title: No foul play in Sigatoka Police officer’s death
item.description: The death of a police officer who was found motionless in Sigatoka Town has been classified as a natural death following a post-mortem examination. Police say the examination found the cause of death was linked to an underlying medical condition, which was exacerbated by personal lifestyle choices.
item.content:encoded:
The death of a police officer who was found motionless in Sigatoka Town has been classified as a natural death following a post-mortem examination.

Police say the examination found the cause of death was linked to an underlying medical condition, which was exacerbated by personal lifestyle choices.

The findings have been communicated to the officer’s next of kin.

The Fiji Police Force says the officer’s death has been the subject of speculation, but the post-mortem examination has ruled out any foul play.

Police are urging members of the public to respect the family’s privacy as they grieve during this difficult time.

item.title: Kepa urges caution
item.description: ROKO Tui Dreketi Ro Teimumu Kepa has urged the Government not to repeat the mistake of “counting its chickens before they hatch” as it seeks parliamentary support to advance Fiji’s constitutional referendum process. Speaking during the Rewa Provincial Council meeting this week, Ro Teimumu said Minister for Rural and Maritime Development and Disaster Management Mosese Bulitavu appeared confident th
item.content:encoded:
ROKO Tui Dreketi Ro Teimumu Kepa has urged the Government not to repeat the mistake of “counting its chickens before they hatch” as it seeks parliamentary support to advance Fiji’s constitutional referendum process.

Speaking during the Rewa Provincial Council meeting this week, Ro Teimumu said Minister for Rural and Maritime Development and Disaster Management Mosese Bulitavu appeared confident the Government would secure the numbers needed in Parliament.

“He seems certain that they will get the numbers, but you know in everything we just have to tell them to pray about it,” she said.

“The last time they were counting their chickens before it was hatched because they thought it would be a walkthrough and walkover.”

The Government’s first attempt to amend the 2013 Constitution failed in March 2025 after falling one vote short of the required 75 per cent parliamentary majority.

The Bill required 41 votes to proceed but received 40 votes in favour and 14 against, while one MP did not vote.

Following the defeat, Cabinet referred constitutional questions to the Supreme Court under Section 91(5) of the Constitution.

In its advisory opinion, the Supreme Court held that constitutional amendments should require a two-thirds majority in Parliament instead of 75 per cent and a simple majority of votes cast in a referendum, rather than 75 per cent of all registered voters.

Ro Teimumu said she hoped the Government would secure the parliamentary support needed so the decision could ultimately rest with the people.

“So many of us want changes in the Constitution and it can only come about through the parliamentary process and also the referendum.”

item.title: Family mourns fallen officer
item.description: VUNAVUTU, Nadroga villager Naomi Kelea says she was devastated upon hearing of the death of Lami police officer Jovesa Tanikorolevu on Thursday morning. Speaking to this newspaper in Sigatoka yesterday, Ms Kelea said the victim was a close friend of her eldest son and had become part of their family.
item.content:encoded:
VUNAVUTU, Nadroga villager Naomi Kelea says she was devastated upon hearing of the death of Lami police officer Jovesa Tanikorolevu on Thursday morning.

Speaking to this newspaper in Sigatoka yesterday, Ms Kelea said the victim was a close friend of her eldest son and had become part of their family.

“I treated Jovesa as my own son as he would come home and stay with us,” she said.

“It was during these trips to our house in Vunavutu that he met his wife, Litiana, who is from Qereqere Village.

“Jovesa was a good rugby player, and he would train with the High-Performance Unit (HPU) in Sigatoka.”

Ms Kelea described Mr Tanikorolevu as a kind and thoughtful person who did not forget their family, even after getting married.

“When he would come to Sigatoka to visit his children and wife at Qereqere Village, he would also visit us at home. I am shocked that he is no longer with us.”

Ms Kelea said she did not know the circumstances surrounding the death but hoped justice would be served.

Police confirmed to The Fiji Times yesterday that the matter was being investigated by the Criminal Investigations Department.

Mr Tanikorolevu’s death is the second involving an officer from the Lami Police Station, following the death of Police Constable Peniasi Racagi in February.

Mr Tanikorolevu is survived by his wife and six children.

He was found lying motionless in Sigatoka Town in the early hours of Thursday.

item.title: Ali urges young women to embrace opportunities
item.description: CHRISTINE Parveena Ali believes young women who are open to new opportunities can lay the foundation for future success. Represented by Guard Force, Ms Ali is one of 10 contestants vying for the title of Nadi International Airport Miss Bula 2026. She has maternal links to Vunitogoloa, Rakiraki.
item.content:encoded:
CHRISTINE Parveena Ali believes young women who are open to new opportunities can lay the foundation for future success.

Represented by Guard Force, Ms Ali is one of 10 contestants vying for the title of Nadi International Airport Miss Bula 2026. She has maternal links to Vunitogoloa, Rakiraki.

Despite being briefly ill, Ms Ali remained committed and attended the remaining contestant engagements.

Ms Ali said she entered the competition to step out of her comfort zone and become a voice for women who may not be able to share what they are going through.

“My advocacy topic is the rising HIV cases among youths in Fiji,” she said.

Ms Ali is an aviation security officer based at Nadi International Airport and has already mapped out her plans if she is crowned Miss Bula 2026.

“I would like to inspire the people of Nadi to not step back but forward and to be courageous,” she said.

“I would inspire the little girls and young women to believe in themselves, trust the process and have faith in God, and there’s so many things that I would love to tell the public but first of all, they need to believe in themselves and step out of their comfort zone to achieve better opportunities.”

item.content:encoded:
THE controversial Momi Bay land swap deal of 2006 has resurfaced with landowners making another last-ditch effort to get the Coalition Government to review the 20-year-old agreement.

The deal made between the Tokatoka o Nahau of Tau Village in Nadroga and the then Laisenia Qarase government allowed the conversion of more than 200 acres of iTaukei land to crown, and then to freehold land, giving way to the Momi Bay development project by then New Zealand-based Matapo Ltd.

The agreement, however, was permanently altered after the 2006 coup, and the implementation of the 2010 Momi Bay Decree which provided an iron clad legal barrier.

The land has since been owned by the Fiji National Provident Fund through its subsidiary – Momi Bay Resort Ltd (MBRL).

This week the landowners and supporters made a public plea for State intervention and for a review of the original agreement.

Spokesperson and Viti Indigenous Tourism Alliance president Sitiveni Leseitoga Nawaqa said turning to the Coalition Government was a last resort.

“We have exhausted all avenues available to us,” said Mr Nawaqa.

“So, we are appealing to Government, to the Prime Minister, Lands Minister, iTaukei Affairs Minister for assistance because this matter has gone on for far too long.

“Now the members of Tokatoka o Nahau don’t want the land swap but their own land back and for it to be converted back to iTaukei land.

“We’ve written to the TLTB, the iTaukei Affairs Ministry, the Prime Ministers Office and the Lands Ministry but we have not received any response from them.

“We even went to lawyers, but they said they could not help us.

In a statement earlier this week, Mr Nawaqa called on the Coalition Government for a review of the original deal.

He said landowners called for direct engagement between the Government, the iTaukei Land Trust Board, FNPF, MBRL and the Tokatoka Nahau leadership.

“We also want public clarification of the current legal status of the land and any obligations arising from the original agreement and consideration of a fair and equitable resolution if outstanding commitments are identified.”

In response, Minister for Lands Filimoni Vosarogo acknowledged the concerns raised by traditional landowners over the 2005 land swap associated with the Momi Bay Marriott Hotel development.

He said the Government inherited a complex issue and was committed to addressing it “responsibly and in good faith”. “Our Coalition Government has inherited this complex issue and is determined to approach it with fairness, transparency, and respect for all parties involved,” Mr Vosarogo said.

Questions sent to Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka, Lands Minister Filimoni Vosarogo, TLTB and FNPF remained unanswered.
